title: Al-Jabbar, the Compeller
hookLine: the Compeller, who also mends what is broken, the way a bone is set
tomorrow: if He's the one who mends what's broken, what's left for pride?

cards: A cast on a broken wrist, covered in marker signatures from the whole class. Underneath, the bone has been set and is held still until it knits. Arabic has a word for that setting: jabr.
And today's name grows from the same root. Pickthall's list in Surah al-Hashr calls Al-Jabbar the Compeller. So which is it: the One who compels, or the One who sets broken bones?

teach.b: Scholars have read the name both ways and held them together. Al-Jabbar is the One whose will nothing resists. And Al-Jabbar is the One who mends: who sets what is broken and makes up what is missing.
The power and the mending are the same hand. Muslims ask for it inside the prayer.
Between the two prostrations, Tirmidhi records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying: forgive me, have mercy on me, mend me, guide me, provide for me. Mend me: wajburni, the same root.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: HE BINDS UP WOUNDS.
teach.b: Now a neighbor who says something close. The Psalms, sung by Jews and Christians, say in the King James words: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
And in Luke's Gospel, Jesus reads from Isaiah: he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted.
What's shared: a God who doesn't only rule over broken things, but binds them up.
An honest difference: for Christians, that healing is seen above all in Jesus himself; for Muslims, Al-Jabbar's mending belongs to Allah alone, asked for directly, between two prostrations.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the name translated the Compeller shares its root with setting a bone.

how: In the sitting between the two prostrations of each prayer unit, many Muslims say a short du'a that includes wajburni, mend me.

o: the Avenger, who punishes every wrongdoer
the Compeller, who also mends what is broken
the Giant, who frightens the proud and strong

games.q: the One who mends — tap the pairs.

s: Al-Jabbar only means the One who forces
scholars read it as the Compeller and the One who mends, held together.
a du'a between the prostrations asks: mend me
Tirmidhi records wajburni, mend me, from the same root.
Muslims and Christians understand God's healing in exactly the same way
both speak of God binding up the broken; Christians see it above all in Jesus, Muslims ask Allah alone directly.

games.q: two friends had a fight and stopped talking. one asks you to 'just make them be friends again.' what does Al-Jabbar's mending look like for you?
o: help set one piece back, gently, then give it time to knit.
make them talk tonight; mending means forcing it to happen now.
stay out of it; once a friendship breaks it can't be fixed.
games.why: a bone is set and then held still while it knits. the mending is real, and it takes time.

practice: Find one small broken thing within reach: a loose thread, a torn page, a fraying cable, a crooked frame. Mend it as well as you can in a minute, with tape, a knot or a careful hand.
For the sit, hold the mended thing and notice it still does its job.

wordCard.voice: Al-Jabbar: the Compeller, whose will none resists, who also mends what is broken.

orig.note: Arabic: the Compeller, who also mends; from j-b-r, the root of setting a bone.

carryVoice: The line for today: he mends, and what he mends still bears weight. See you tomorrow.
